question: Is the renunciation of action or the yoga of action better? (BhG 3.1–8, 5.1–6, 6.1–4, 18.1–12)

sides.position: As reported at BhG 18.3a (holders unnamed, 'some thinkers'): action is to be abandoned as faulty.
As reported at BhG 18.3b (holders unnamed, 'others'): acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be abandoned.

Kṛṣṇa's stated conclusion (18.4–12): sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be abandoned but done, giving up attachment and fruit; renouncing obligatory action is improper; relinquishment is threefold; since the embodied cannot give up action entirely, the relinquisher of fruit is the true relinquisher, and the fruit of action does not accrue to renouncers.
arguments: Sacrifice, giving and austerity purify the wise (18.5).
The embodied cannot give up actions entirely (18.11).
Abandoning obligatory action from delusion is tāmasic, from fear of hardship rājasic (18.7–8).

notes: Extractor A records only the sides as ch. 18 states them; the text itself names no holders of the two reported views (commentators' attributions are theirs).

question: Should Arjuna fight the battle in which his elders, teachers and kinsmen stand on the other side?

sides.position: Arjuna's resolve 'I will not fight', as Kṛṣṇa recalls it at the close (18.59).

Kṛṣṇa at the close: that resolve, made from the sense of 'I', is vain; Arjuna's nature will compel him, and bound by his nature-born action he will act even unwillingly (18.59–60); one without the sense of doership does not slay though slaying (18.17).

historical_debates.name: The dialogue at Kurukṣetra
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Arjuna declares his delusion destroyed and his doubts gone, and says 'I will do your word' (18.73); Sañjaya holds that where Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are there is victory (18.78).

notes: Contribution of the closing chunk only; the opening sides are in chs. 1–3.
